articles.title: Rochdale Council leaves door open for Hopwood Hall reconciliation after court ruling
articles.excerpt: Following a recent High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has expressed willingness to engage with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, which has been a point of contention since the termination of their agreement in 2024.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has indicated a willingness to engage in discussions with filmmaker Hopwood DePree regarding the future of Hopwood Hall, following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate their agreement.

This development comes after a two-day trial at Manchester Civil Justice Centre in September, where the court ruled that the council acted lawfully in ending the exclusivity agreement with DePree, who had sought to purchase the historic site for £1.

The council's option agreement with DePree, which began in 2017, was terminated in October 2024, leading to a legal dispute. DePree, who claims ancestral ties to the hall, believed he had a binding agreement to purchase the property.

However, the court found that a planning approval granted in 2022 did not trigger the option to buy the hall for the nominal fee.

In response to the court's decision, DePree has issued an open letter to the council, outlining his terms for a potential resolution.

He expressed a desire for constructive dialogue and transparency regarding the council's decisions, including a request for the release of documents related to the handling of the hall's management. DePree has suggested that an independent review could help clarify the situation and facilitate discussions.

Council leader Neil Emmott reiterated that the council's 'door is always open' for DePree to present a viable plan for Hopwood Hall's future.

Both parties have acknowledged that the costly court battle could have been avoided, and there is hope for an amicable resolution that benefits the community and preserves the historic site.

articles.title: Littleborough Christmas lights: Church Street restrictions confirmed for 28 November
articles.excerpt: Church Street restrictions are planned for Littleborough's Christmas lights event on Saturday 28 November, including a daytime waiting ban and an afternoon road closure.
articles.content_html:
Drivers and visitors heading into Littleborough for the Christmas lights event on Saturday, 28 November 2026 should plan around temporary restrictions on Church Street.

Rochdale Borough Council's published traffic notice says a road closure will operate from 1.30pm until 7pm. A prohibition on waiting is due to run from noon until 7pm on the same day, meaning parking arrangements will change before the road closure starts.

The notice identifies Church Street and Peel Street as the location of the restriction. Its wording for the precise starting junction is unclear, because it describes Church Street as beginning at a junction with Church Street itself. Residents who need access to a particular property should check the official notice and seek clarification from the council rather than relying on an assumed boundary.

The council lists Church Street, Morgan Street, Peel Street and Station Road as the alternative route. Drivers should follow temporary signs on the day, as the published notice does not provide a street-by-street map of how each turning will operate.

The restrictions are for the Littleborough Christmas Lights Event 2026, which the council has confirmed for Saturday, 28 November. The traffic notice does not give the entertainment timetable or the exact time of the lights switch-on, so those details should not be assumed from the road closure hours.

Anyone planning to visit shops, businesses or homes around the affected streets should allow extra time, particularly during the afternoon and early evening. Those with deliveries or access requirements may wish to confirm arrangements ahead of the event.

The full council notice, including the restriction wording and alternative route, can be checked at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2626/littleborough-christmas-lights-event-2026-road-closures-in-littleborough-on-28-november-2026.

articles.title: Rochdale to review future primary and secondary school place needs on 24 November
articles.excerpt: The council's forward plan schedules reports on primary places through 2030 and secondary places through 2031, alongside high-needs investment, for its 24 November cabinet meeting.
articles.content_html:
How many school places will Rochdale need in the next few years? The borough council has scheduled separate reports on primary and secondary capacity for consideration by its cabinet on Tuesday, 24 November 2026.

The council's official forward plan lists 'Need for Primary School Places 2027–2030' and 'Need for Secondary School Places 2027–2031'. Both are assigned to lead officer Fay Davies and marked as open rather than exempt items. The same meeting is due to consider a 'High Needs Capital and Investment 2026' report, which is marked part exempt because of financial or commercially sensitive information.

These are proposed decision dates, not announcements of new schools, closures, catchment changes or a confirmed number of places. The forward plan identifies subjects the council expects to consider, but it does not itself contain the detailed forecasts, recommendations or decisions. Those must be checked in the published agenda papers when available.

The timing matters to parents thinking ahead to admissions in 2027 and beyond. School-place planning looks at the capacity required across future years, while an individual child's application and allocation follow the separate admissions process. The council's published secondary-school application deadline for September 2027 entry was Saturday, 31 October 2026; families who missed it should use the council's admissions guidance rather than assuming the forthcoming cabinet report changes the deadline.

Other open items listed for 24 November include additional highway maintenance funding, a community asset transfer policy and the calculation of the 2027/28 Council Tax base. The plan also schedules a capital programme for consultation and discretionary fees and charges for consultation for 30 November, with the borough Local Plan publication plan listed for 17 December. These dates can change and do not establish that any proposal has been approved.

Rochdale Daily will check the agenda and published reports before reporting any school-place figures, recommended changes or financial commitments. Residents can read the official forward plan and subsequent meeting papers through the council's democratic services website.

Primary source: Rochdale Borough Council, Notice of Key Decisions and Private Items, 1 October 2026 to 31 January 2027: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgListPlanItems.aspx?PlanId=1453.

articles.title: Heywood’s Little Play Town put up for sale as owner reassures families it will stay open
articles.excerpt: Owner Jackie is seeking a buyer after four years, with Little Play Town remaining open and existing party bookings going ahead as planned.
articles.content_html:
Little Play Town in Heywood has been put up for sale, with owner Jackie reassuring families that the children’s role play business will remain open and existing party bookings will go ahead as planned.

Announcing the decision, Jackie said she was selling for personal reasons after four years of building the business alongside her team.

“This is something I never thought I’d be writing, and it’s been an incredibly difficult decision to make,” she said.

Jackie described Little Play Town as her “pride and joy” and thanked the staff, customers and families who have supported it.

She stressed that the sale announcement does not mean the venue is closing. Sessions will continue as normal, and families with parties booked do not need to change their plans.

The search is now on for a new owner to take over the established leasehold business. Jackie said a support package lasting up to three months would be available to help the buyer settle in.

The announcement highlights the existing staff team, supportive customer base and opportunities to introduce additional themed events, sessions and experiences. Jackie also described the landlord as proactive and supportive.

She hopes to find someone who will build on the business’s first four years and continue providing a place for children to play and make memories.

Anyone interested in buying Little Play Town can register their interest by emailing info@littleplaytownheywood.co.uk.

articles.title: Rochdale Asda worker's kindness a 'breath of fresh air' for widowed customer
articles.excerpt: Shaheda times her help around an older customer's shopping trips after the woman lost her husband, scanning and packing her shopping and stopping for a chat.
articles.content_html:
A worker at Asda's Rochdale store has been praised for looking out for an older customer after the woman was widowed.

Shaheda first noticed something had changed when the customer, who used to shop with her husband, stopped coming in for a while. When she next saw her, the woman was shopping with her daughter, and the pair told her what had happened.

The daughter lives in London and was worried about how her mother would cope on her own. Shaheda promised to look after her and told her which days she works, so the customer could time her visits for when Shaheda would be there.

Now, when the customer comes in, Shaheda scans and packs her shopping, fetches her a chair and makes time for a chat.

The customer told the store's customer manager, Dave, how much the help meant to her. Dave said: "The lady told me that ever since she lost her husband three months ago, Shaheda has been like a breath of fresh air in her life every time she shops – not just because of the help she offers, but as an emotional support and somebody to chat to."

Shaheda said: "I used to see the lady come in with her husband all the time and then didn't see her for a while. Then I saw her shopping with her daughter, and they told me what had happened. I told her to come and see me every time she came in... and she does. We have a good chat and I help her, as she does struggle a bit."

She added: "She thanks me every single time and I go, 'no, you don't need to thank me'. It's sweet, though. I like to think that somebody would do that for my own mum. I always think too that one day I could be in that position. It doesn't cost anything to be pleasant and kind, does it?"

For someone adjusting to life alone after a bereavement, a familiar face on a weekly errand can make a real difference, and the help Shaheda gives costs nothing but a little time.

articles.title: Plans approved for 27 affordable homes in Rochdale town centre
articles.excerpt: Great Places Housing Group's proposal for 27 affordable homes on Drake Street has received approval from Rochdale Council, aiming to address local housing needs.
articles.content_html:
Plans for 27 new affordable homes in Rochdale town centre have been approved by Rochdale Council.

The development, proposed by Great Places Housing Group, will be located on vacant land at 206-208 Drake Street, which has been unused for several years after the demolition of a former DVLA test centre.

The approved scheme includes a three-storey apartment building with 23 apartments and a 2.5-storey terrace of four family homes.

The site, situated at the corner of Drake Street and Broadfield Stile, is adjacent to the Grade II-registered Broadfield Park, providing good access to local services and public transport.

Supporting documents from Paddock Johnson architects highlight that the project will provide 100% affordable housing for social rent, exceeding local policy requirements and responding to an identified housing need within Rochdale.

The redevelopment aims to make effective use of an underused urban site, contributing to the local community's housing stock.

The council previously granted planning permission on appeal for a different scheme of 17 homes, which did not proceed. The new development is expected to enhance the area and provide substantial public benefit, with construction timelines yet to be confirmed.

Great Places Housing Group applied to Rochdale Council to create a development of 27 affordable dwellings, including a three-storey apartment building containing 23 apartments, and a 2.5-storey terrace of four family homes on the land at 206-208 Drake Street. articles.title: Eighth arrest in property damage investigation covering Rochdale
articles.excerpt: GMP says Rochdale is among six areas where properties were damaged during October. A 29-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.
articles.content_html:
An investigation into damage to properties in Rochdale and five other Greater Manchester areas has led to an eighth arrest, police have said.

A 29-year-old man was arrested on Monday morning, 2 November, on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage. Greater Manchester Police said he was being questioned in connection with damage caused during October.

The force said the wider investigation concerns houses in multiple occupation, known as HMOs, and properties mistaken for HMOs.

Since 5 October, police have been made aware of damage to buildings in Rochdale, Salford, Tameside, Stockport, Bolton and Wigan. The latest release does not identify the Rochdale properties or give a separate total for the borough.

GMP said the arrest brought the number of people detained during the investigation to eight. GMP has not given the location of the latest arrest.

Enquiries are continuing. Anyone with information that could help the investigation can contact police on 101 or report it online at https://www.gmp.police.uk/.

Information can also be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

The arrest is not a finding of guilt. The man is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

articles.title: Rochdale Sixth Form College to host Open Evening on 19 November
articles.excerpt: Prospective students and families are invited to explore courses and meet staff at Rochdale Sixth Form College's Open Evening.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Sixth Form College will host an Open Evening on Thursday, 19 November, from 4pm to 7pm. This event is aimed at prospective students and their families, providing an opportunity to explore the college's offerings and learn more about its academic environment.

Visitors can meet experienced tutors, speak with current Student Ambassadors, and discover the wide range of A level and vocational courses available.

The college is recognised as one of the leading sixth form providers in the UK, particularly noted for its value-added performance, which reflects the progress students make during their studies.

The Principal’s Talk will take place at multiple times throughout the evening, specifically at 4:30pm, 5:15pm, and 6pm. Attendees are encouraged to arrive at the Theatre on the first floor about ten minutes before their chosen session.

There is no need to book a separate place for the talk, allowing flexibility for visitors to attend whichever session suits them best.

To attend the Open Evening, places must be booked in advance. Interested parties can register and find more information by visiting the college's official website.

Please note that there is no on-site parking available, so visitors are advised to check nearby parking options before arriving.

articles.title: Sandbrook Way KFC licence now permits late-night service until 5am
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's public licensing register shows updated permission for late-night refreshment at the Sandbrook Way KFC, with the restaurant area due to close at midnight under a licence condition.
articles.content_html:
The KFC at Sandbrook Way, Edinburgh Way, Rochdale, has a premises licence permitting late-night refreshment until 5am on every day of the week, according to Rochdale Borough Council's public licensing register.

The register identifies the premises as KFC, OL11 1RY, and names Chicken Cabins Ltd trading as KFC as the licence holder. It lists licence PL(N)1021 with an effective date of 17 October 2026. The permitted premises hours are shown as 10am to 5am, while late-night refreshment is authorised from 11pm to 5am, indoors and outdoors.

There is an important distinction between the permission and what customers can expect on any particular night. The licence sets out what is legally authorised; it is not a verified announcement that every service is operating throughout those hours. A condition in the published record says the restaurant area is to close at midnight, with delivery and drive-through service afterwards.

An earlier version of the same council record, viewed as at 11 October 2026, listed midnight closing on most days and 1am on Friday and Saturday. The updated register therefore records a materially later authorised finish time. It does not explain the commercial reasons for the change or give a launch date for extended service.

The licence includes conditions covering CCTV, door supervision during late-night licensing hours, management of noise and litter, and requests for customers to leave quietly. These are licence requirements, not evidence of a specific incident at the premises.

Customers wanting to know whether collection, drive-through or delivery is currently available after midnight should check directly with the restaurant. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the operator confirms its actual trading timetable.

Primary source: Rochdale Borough Council's live licensing register, premises licence PL(N)1021: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/2860/Detail?LIC_ID=22977.

articles.title: Free play sessions for young children in Littleborough and Middleton this week
articles.excerpt: Littleborough Library has a free under-fives session on Tuesday 3 November, while Junction Library in Middleton is advertising Saturday Lego and Duplo play for children aged two and over.
articles.content_html:
Families looking for free activities with young children this week have two council-listed library sessions to consider in Littleborough and Middleton, with no advance booking required for either.

Littleborough Library, at Hare Hill Park, OL15 9HE, is advertising Library Time for Tuesday, 3 November 2026, from 9.15am to 10.15am. The session is aimed at children under five with their parents, carers or childminders. It offers toys, puppets, simple crafts and a chance to meet other families. The council describes Library Time as an every-other-Tuesday activity, and says visitors can simply turn up.

In Middleton, Junction Library on Grimshaw Lane, M24 2BW, is advertising Lego and Duplo play on Saturday, 7 November, from 10am until noon. It is a free weekly activity for families with children aged two and over. No booking is needed. The council explains that it is informal creative play rather than a structured Lego class; children can choose to have their creations displayed at the library.

The two sessions serve different age groups and take place on different days. Parents should check the council's current event listings before travelling, particularly if a session is affected by an unexpected change to library opening or staffing.

The libraries also offer books and other reading activities, and the council maintains a wider events directory for families who cannot attend either session. A free library session does not require families to buy materials or tickets for the activities described above.

Official details: Littleborough Library Time, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/258/library-time---littleborough-library; Junction Library Lego and Duplo play, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/503/lego-and-duplo-play-on-saturdays---junction-library. articles.title: Rochdale driver jailed for 16 months after dangerous police pursuit
articles.excerpt: Bilal Ishaq admitted four driving offences after a pursuit through Rochdale. Police say he ran red lights and twice tried to reverse into pursuing vehicles.
articles.content_html:
A disqualified driver who fled police through Rochdale has been jailed for 16 months and banned from driving for five years.

Bilal Ishaq, 34, of Hey Street, Rochdale, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, failing to stop and driving without insurance, Greater Manchester Police said in a release issued on 2 November.

Officers had tried to stop a vehicle on Foxholes Road in September. GMP said the vehicle was linked to suspected drug dealing. The offences set out in the force’s sentencing announcement were driving offences.

Ishaq drove away, beginning a pursuit through the town. According to police, he reached speeds more than three times the limit, went through red lights and drove on the wrong side of the road.

The force said he also tried to reverse into pursuing police vehicles on two occasions. After crashing, he attempted to run away but was detained by officers.

GMP said Ishaq was already subject to two driving disqualifications imposed in January 2026 following a separate dangerous driving incident in December 2025.

PC Matt Balkwell, from the force’s Motorcycle Unit, said: “His actions could easily have resulted in serious injury or loss of life.”

The officer praised the work of those involved in detaining Ishaq and said police would continue to pursue drivers who endangered their communities.

articles.content_html:
Residents of Halifax Road in Rochdale have been allowed to return to their homes after a car crashed into a house early on Saturday morning, October 31, 2026, causing a gas leak. The incident occurred shortly before 3am, prompting a swift response from emergency services.

Greater Manchester Police reported that they received calls about the collision at around 2:55am. The crash resulted in a confirmed gas leak, leading to the evacuation of approximately 55 residents from nearby properties.

A 50-metre cordon was established while investigations were conducted and safety measures were put in place.

Three fire engines from Rochdale and Littleborough fire stations attended the scene, where firefighters worked to secure the area and assist with evacuations. Two individuals were taken to hospital by the North West Ambulance Service, although their conditions have not been disclosed.

Emergency services remained on-site for about four-and-a-half hours to manage the situation.

Following the containment of the gas leak, Halifax Road has since reopened, allowing residents to return home. This incident underscores the critical role of emergency services in ensuring public safety during unexpected events.

articles.title: Rochdale reception school applications for 2027: deadline, preferences and offer dates
articles.excerpt: Parents applying for a Rochdale borough reception place starting September 2027 have until 15 January. The council has also confirmed the offer date and rules for school preferences.
articles.content_html:
Applications for reception places at Rochdale borough primary schools for September 2027 are open, with parents and carers given until Friday, 15 January 2027 to apply on time.

Rochdale Borough Council opened its online admissions system on 14 September 2026. The council says parents should submit their application before the January closing date; otherwise, it will be treated as late. National offer day for reception places is Friday, 16 April 2027, when families can find out which school has been offered.

Parents are encouraged to name five different schools in their order of preference. Listing only one school does not improve the chance of being offered that school. If it is oversubscribed, the published admissions criteria are applied; where a preferred school cannot be offered, the council considers the other preferences and available places.

The council advises families to check each school's admissions policy before applying. The rules for community and voluntary controlled schools are not necessarily the same as those for academies, foundation or voluntary aided schools. Attending a school's nursery class does not normally guarantee priority for its reception class. Some schools also ask parents to submit supplementary forms directly to the school.

For families who move house after applying, the council lists Friday, 12 February 2027 as the final date for address changes to be considered in the initial allocation, subject to the required evidence. Changes of school preference after the application deadline are treated as late.

Parents considering deferring their child's start should still apply by 15 January. The council explains that the rules depend on the child's birthday, and applications for a place outside the normal age group require supporting evidence and an individual decision by the admission authority.

Children living in Rochdale borough apply through Rochdale Borough Council even when choosing a school outside the borough. Families who live elsewhere must apply through their own council. The school admissions team can be contacted at school.admissions@rochdale.gov.uk or 0300 303 0340.

Full dates, admissions guidance and the application route are published at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/school-admissions-appeals/apply-primary-school-place. Families can also consult the council's guidance before choosing schools at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/school-admissions-appeals/apply-primary-school-place/3.

articles.title: Birthday cards for Wendy: family’s heartfelt appeal ahead of her 79th birthday
articles.excerpt: Wendy Bamford turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November, and her birthday wish is simple: cards filled with kind words.
articles.content_html:
A family is inviting the community to help make Wendy Bamford’s 79th birthday special by sending her a card filled with a few kind words.

Wendy turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November. Her son Stephen Bamford shared the appeal after she moved to Springhill Hospice in Rochdale.

When he asked his mum what she wanted for her birthday, or whether there was anything she would like to do, her answer was simple: lots of birthday cards, so she could sit and read the lovely messages inside. It is the only thing she has asked for, Stephen said.

A little kindness could mean so much

Stephen is welcoming cards from people who know Wendy and those who have never met her but would like to brighten her day.

“A few kind words might seem like a small thing, but they would mean the world to her right now,” he wrote.

In an update, Stephen thanked everyone for their comments and messages, explaining that the response had become too large for him to answer individually. He shared two addresses where cards can be sent.

Where to send a birthday card

Cards can be addressed directly to Wendy at:

Wendy Bamford, Room 10, Springhill Hospice, Broad Lane, Rochdale

Alternatively, cards can be sent to Stephen through the Littleborough collection address:

For Wendy Bamford, care of Stephen Bamford, Cryers Butchers, 39 Victoria Street, Littleborough, OL15 8BA

Stephen has promised to make sure his mum receives them, ready to open and enjoy on her birthday. Anyone wishing to take part is encouraged to allow time for delivery.

articles.title: Middleton schools face financial challenges due to declining pupil numbers
articles.excerpt: Middleton schools are grappling with financial pressures as a significant drop in birth rates is expected to impact primary school enrolments in 2027.
articles.content_html:
Middleton schools are facing financial challenges as a report reveals a significant decline in birth rates, which is expected to affect primary school enrolments in 2027.

The report, presented to township committees, highlights that the borough is experiencing the lowest birth rate for 23 years, leading to concerns about the long-term financial sustainability of some primary schools.

In September 2026, there was a peak in Reception year pupils, but the projected intake for 2027 is only 2,647, the lowest since 2003.

This decline is anticipated to create additional financial pressures for schools that have already seen a reduction in student numbers and an increase in empty seats over recent years.

The report indicates that while there has been an average of 113 children needing places after moving into the borough each year, this figure has dropped to just 20 over the past two years.

An average of 30 pupils per year have not taken up secondary school places within the borough, exacerbating the situation.

As a response to the declining numbers, Rochdale Council has already removed 90 surplus Reception places for September 2024 and an additional 35 for September 2025.

Further reductions are expected in areas where there are too many empty places, highlighting the need for strategic planning to address these challenges.

The report said: “A small number of schools have seen too many empty seats over the last few years as intake numbers reduced and a low intake in 2027 is going to see additional financial pressures on those schools. “Current birth rates indicate a steady but slow rise in the years to 2030. The current projected intake for 2030 is approximately 2,900 and includes children from new housing developments across the borough.” In September, 2024, 90 surplus Reception places were removed, followed by an additional 35 for September, 2025. The report warns that further reductions are needed in some areas of the borough where there are too many empty places. While recent years have seen an average of 113 children needing places after moving into the borough each year, this figure has fallen to 20 over the past two years. As well as fewer children entering primary schools, there has been an average of 30 pupils per year not taking up secondary school places within the borough. On offer day, 2,860 pupils were offered places in Rochdale’s secondary schools. Of those offers, 2,485 were offered their first-choice school, 290 were offered a school that they had named as a preference, and 85 were offered a school that was not a preference. A total of 322 children also put as their first preference one of the ten most popular out-of-borough schools. The net number of pupils moving to out of borough this year at transition was 304. This is similar to last year when 310 left for out-of-borough schools. Boroughwide secondary intakes were unexpectedly lower this year. The forecast is for 2027 to be the largest secondary intake year with 3,015 pupils expected to apply to secondary schools within the borough offering 3,060 places. The issues will be highlighted at Heywood Township Committee on Monday, Pennines Township Committee on Tuesday, Rochdale North Township Committee on Wednesday and Middleton Township Committee on Thursday. articles.title: Rochdale Council approves new Storage World building in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for a new Storage World building in Middleton, following a fire that destroyed the previous structure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has approved the rebuilding of Storage World in Middleton town centre. The planning application submitted by Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd (SSPMI) was greenlit to replace the building on Old Hall Street, which was destroyed by fire in June last year.

The new development will be a £12 million mixed-use building, smaller in footprint but taller than the previous structure.

It will feature self-storage units on the upper floors and commercial units on the ground floor, occupying half the space of the former Storage World but with two additional storeys to maintain capacity.

In their application, P4 Planning highlighted the aim to create a modern design that would not only restore self-storage services but also stimulate small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) activity in the area.

They noted that the design would reflect the historical context of the site, which previously housed Albany Mill until 1975.

This development is expected to contribute positively to the regeneration of Middleton town centre, enhancing the local economy and providing much-needed facilities for residents and businesses alike.

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract for the management and support services of the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme (HFLS) to The Bond Board Limited.

This contract, published on Find a Tender, aims to provide essential tenancy management and support services for homeless families placed in temporary accommodation.

The HFLS will manage approximately 40 leased properties, ensuring that families receive the necessary support to sustain their tenancies. Services will include property management, tenancy sustainment, and move-on support, which are crucial for helping families transition to permanent housing.

This initiative is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of homelessness in Rochdale. By providing structured support, the council aims to improve the living conditions of vulnerable families and reduce the number of families experiencing homelessness in the borough.

The Bond Board Limited is expected to begin its services shortly, although specific timelines for the implementation of the HFLS have not been disclosed. This development highlights the council's commitment to tackling homelessness and supporting families in need.

Actor Mark Winstanley is set to return to the stage after a five-year break following his diagnosis with multiple sclerosis. He will perform in 'Cabaret Schmabaret' at the Ukrainian Centre in Rochdale on 19 November, bringing his comedic talents back to the local audience.

Winstanley, who co-runs the Manchester-based theatre company The Performers’ Playground with Alice Robinson, has a rich history in theatre, having performed nationally and internationally with various touring companies.

His return is particularly significant as it showcases his resilience and commitment to the arts despite his health challenges.

In addition to 'Cabaret Schmabaret', The Performers’ Playground is also fundraising for a separate production of 'Ubu Royale', which is currently in research and development. This production is designed to accommodate Winstanley's mobility and fatigue issues, with plans for a national tour in 2027.

Winstanley's comeback not only highlights his personal journey but also serves as an inspiration for others facing similar challenges. Local audiences can look forward to enjoying a unique comedic experience while supporting a talented artist's return to the stage.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.body:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale. The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location. Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record. 

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes. Victorian county compilers and parish historians — the sources relied on by Historic England — record that the medieval Clegg family held land here, but that their holding had changed hands by the late 1200s and that later documentary evidence for a family murder is absent. In short: there is no surviving contemporary legal or parish record that corroborates the tale of an uncle murdering heirs by throwing them into a moat. (These points are set out in the local histories cited in the Historic England listing and in the History of the Parish of Rochdale.)

What the storytellers say: the best‑known version of the boggart appears in 19th‑century folklore collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance. These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage. That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson. Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales. The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on. If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615). For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form). If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records. For now, the boggart is a good story worth retelling — and a reminder to treat nineteenth‑century folklore as a literary and cultural source, not a court roll.

John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance.

These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage.

That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson.

Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales.

The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on.

If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615).

For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form).

If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records.

For now, the boggart is a good story worth retelling — and a reminder to treat nineteenth‑century folklore as a literary and cultural source, not a court roll.
